name: Computer music
editorial_article: Computer music represents the foundational intersection of computational science and musical composition, acting as a broad field of study and artistic practice that encompasses sound synthesis, algorithmic composition, and digital signal processing. Unlike traditional instrumentation, which relies on physical sound production, computer music leverages the power of logic and binary systems to model, generate, and manipulate audio at the microscopic level of the waveform. The field emerged in the late 1940s and early 1950s, not as a commercial genre but as a series of experiments by pioneers at institutions like Bell Labs and university computer centers. Early milestones included the CSIRAC in Australia and the Ferranti Mark 1 in England, which performed the first recorded instances of computer-generated melodies. \n\nThroughout the 1960s and 1970s, the field shifted from primitive tone generation to the development of sophisticated synthesis architectures. Figures such as Max Mathews, who created the MUSIC-N series, and John Chowning, whose work on frequency modulation (FM) synthesis became a cornerstone of modern digital sound, redefined the relationship between composer and machine. This lineage connects the massive, room-sized mainframe computers that required hours of processing time for seconds of audio to the ubiquitous digital audio workstations (DAWs) that define contemporary production. By treating sound as mathematical data, computer music unlocked new possibilities for timbre, spatialization, and generative structures that were previously physically impossible, effectively becoming the bedrock for electronic music culture and contemporary sound art worldwide.
editorial_definition: A multidisciplinary field involving the application of computing technology to musical composition, synthesis, and sound design.
